When a component has one thread of execution, code for only one object can execute at any given time. The Automation feature of the Component Object Model ([[T0]]) deals with this situation by serializing requests. That is, the requests are queued and processed one at a time until all have been completed.

In a multithreading operating environment, serialization protects single-threaded objects from overlapping client requests — that is, from code in a property or method being executed while one or more previous client requests are still being run. Overlapping requests can cause internal data errors if objects aren't designed for reentrancy.

Serialization is thus an extremely important feature of Automation. However, serialization of single-threaded components means that requests are sometimes blocked. For example, suppose you're using a Widget object that has two methods, spin and flip.
 - The Spin method takes anywhere from several seconds to half an hour to complete.
- The Flip method is almost instantaneous.

Because 32-bit applications are preemptively multitasked, a second application could call the Flip method while the Spin method is already running. The short Flip method is blocked until the long Spin method is complete.

When short operations are blocked by long ones, productivity suffers and user frustration rises. Components that behave in this fashion are said to scale poorly. That is, they work poorly if many requests of mixed length are made.

[[T0]] provides two component features to address scalability and avoid blocked calls — SingleUse instancing and multithreaded objects. For details, see Controlling Call Blocking.

You can define variables in the report or label layout for storing, manipulating, and displaying values.

Report variables are [[T0]] in scope, and remain available after a report run (unless you explicitly specify that they should be released).

- Open the report or label in the appropriate designer.
- On the Report menu, click Variables . The Report Properties dialog box opens. Note If the _REPORTBUILDER system variable is not set to the default Report Builder or is set to a third-party builder, the Report Variables dialog box displays or a different dialog box might display. For more information, see _REPORTBUILDER System Variable and Report Variables Dialog Box .
- In the Report Properties dialog box, click the Variables tab if it is not selected.
- On the Variables tab, click Add .
- In the Report Variable dialog box, type the name for the variable.
- In the Value to store box, type an expression. At any given time during the report run, the variable will contain the evaluated results of the expression.
- To specify an initial value for the variable, in the Initial value box, type an type an expression. The evaluated result of this expression will be assigned to the variable at the beginning of the report run.. Note If you use the report variable in calculations, make sure to initialize the variable with a nonzero value to avoid a division-by-zero error. If you do not specify an initial value, [[T0]] assigns a default value of 0.
- To specify additional calculations to perform on the evaluated expression results prior to assigning a value to the variable, in the Calculation type list, select the calculation operation you want.
- For cumulative calculation types, you can also specify the point at which the variable value is reset, by changing the setting of Reset value based on . For detailed information on calculation types, see Calculate Tab, Report Control Properties Dialog Box (Report Builder) .
- When you are finished, click [[T1]] . You can now use the variable in your report or label.

For more information, see Variables Tab, Report Properties Dialog Box (Report Builder).

For example, consider a table of timesheet information with fields for punch-in and punch-out times stored in [[I0]], [[I1]], [[I2]], and [[I3]] fields. The following table shows three example variables used in a report:

| To store this value | Create this variable | Using this expression |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Time employee arrived | [[T0]] | hour_in + (min_in / 60) |
| Time employee left | [[T1]] | hour_out + (min_out / 60) |
| Total time employee was present | [[T2]] | [[T3]] - [[T4]] |

You can use the [[I4]] variable in a variety of other calculations, such as the number of hours worked in a week, a month, or a year; the average number of hours worked each day; and so on.

For examples of report variables, see the sample reports [[T5]] and [[T6]] in the [[T7]] ...\Samples\Solution\Reports directory.
